live.name: ALPHV
live.headline: ALPHV: a ransomware actor known by several names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists ALPHV under several aliases and a set of tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: ALPHV is the main name for this actor in the catalogue record.
It is also listed as ALPHVM, Ambitious Scorpius, BlackCat Gang and UNC4466.
The catalogue links the name to tools including BlackCat, Noberus, Munchkin, Mimikatz, Impacket, PsExec, LaZagne, MEGAsync and GO Simple Tunnel (GOST).
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: ALPHV
next.headline: ALPHV/BlackCat: a ransomware-as-a-service gang built on data theft and leak-site extortion
next.in_short: ALPHV, also called BlackCat, runs a Rust-based ransomware-as-a-service that was first seen in November 2021. It steals data and threatens to publish it. In March 2024 BleepingComputer judged it to be running an exit scam.

sentences.t: ALPHV is also tracked as ALPHVM, BlackCat, BlackCat Gang, Ambitious Scorpius and UNC4466.
Malpedia describes it as a ransomware-as-a-service family written in Rust that runs on Windows, Linux and VMware ESXi.
Malpedia says it has been seen in attacks since November 18, 2021.
BleepingComputer reports that ALPHV is believed to be a rebrand of the DarkSide and BlackMatter operations.

Cisco Talos calls the links to BlackMatter probable. It has moderate confidence that BlackMatter affiliates were among early BlackCat adopters. Talos adds that a BlackCat representative said the groups were connected but that BlackCat was not a rebranding.

BleepingComputer cites the FBI as linking the gang to over 60 breaches in its first four months. It also cites an FBI estimate of at least $300 million in ransom from more than 1,000 victims through September 2023.
eSentire reports that various security teams say the core operators are based in Russia. The report does not verify this itself.
Cybernews reported that BlackCat added NJVC, an IT company supporting US government and defense organisations, to its leak site in September 2022 and then removed it. The claim was not confirmed.

DataBreaches linked a 2022 attack on Suffolk County, which disabled its 911 system, to ALPHV/BlackCat. The group claimed responsibility and claimed 400 GB of data, but the publisher could not confirm the leak.
ALPHV listed the city of Alexandria, Louisiana as a victim. The gang claimed more than 80 GB of data, which is its own claim as quoted in the report.

Recorded Future News reports that Black Cat/AlphV listed Sun Pharmaceuticals, India's largest drugmaker, on its leak site on March 24. The company confirmed a ransomware attack but did not name the group.
BleepingComputer reported that ALPHV claimed breaches of loanDepot and Prudential Financial. The claims were unverified at the time, because the gang had not yet published proof.

Sygnia attributed one 2023 extortion case to BlackCat or one of its affiliates, not to a single confirmed actor. Access came through a compromised third-party vendor. The attacker then used Cobalt Strike for lateral movement, Rclone to copy data to cloud storage, and extortion emails.
In that case the client blocked internet access, which Sygnia says stopped encryption.
eSentire reports that Russian-speaking affiliates used Google ads to lure users to attacker-controlled sites. Victims downloaded the Nitrogen malware, which led to ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware.

Symantec says updates in mid-2022 added an ARM build and safe-mode encryption, and made stolen data searchable on the leak sites. It also saw an affiliate use the Eamfo infostealer against Veeam backup credentials.
Malpedia says the ransomware can encrypt files with AES or ChaCha20 and can delete volume shadow copies. It can also stop ESXi virtual machines and spread to other hosts using PsExec.

In its own statement on the 2023 MGM Resorts attack, AlphV said it kept super administrator access to MGM's Okta. It also said it launched ransomware against more than 100 ESXi hypervisors on September 11. These are the group's own unverified claims.
In the Henry Schein incident, the report says AlphV (BlackCat) claimed responsibility and re-encrypted systems after negotiations broke down.
In November 2023 the group listed Hampton-Newport News CSB on its leak site. It claimed over 800 GB of stolen data and set a 48-hour deadline.
In December 2023 the group claimed a breach at Viking Therapeutics. DataBreaches says the claim is unconfirmed. The group allegedly got an employee to file an SEC complaint about the incident.
BleepingComputer reports that in December 2023 an international law enforcement operation seized the gang's Tor negotiation and leak sites.

In February 2024 BleepingComputer reported that unnamed sources linked the Change Healthcare attack to BlackCat. The outlet could not confirm this, and the gang had not claimed the attack. UnitedHealth's SEC filing described a nation-state threat actor.

In March 2024 BleepingComputer judged that the gang was running an exit scam. Its sites went offline, affiliates said they were not paid, and the gang offered its source code for $5 million. It also posted a fake FBI seizure banner, and Europol and the NCA said they were not involved.
Malpedia lists a December 30, 2025 US Justice Department release saying two Americans pleaded guilty to targeting US victims with ALPHV BlackCat ransomware.
Treat a gang's leak-site claim as unverified until the victim or investigators confirm it.
Keep backup systems and their credentials well separated from everyday administrator accounts.
